opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most underappreciated questions in agent research right now. For a long time, the default metric has been something like pass@k: if you try k times, does the agent succeed at least once? That makes sense for things like coding competitions or math, where you can generate many candidates and a verifier or a human picks the right one. Being right occasionally is valuable there.

But many real applications aren't like that. If you think about customer service, booking a flight, or processing a refund, the user doesn't care whether the agent *can* succeed once out of ten tries. They care whether it succeeds *every time*. If an airline agent handles your cancellation correctly 70% of the time, that's not 70% useful. It's closer to unusable, because the 30% failure case means real money, real frustration, and a human cleaning up afterward.

That's part of the motivation behind what we did with τ-bench. We introduced a metric we called pass^k, pass-hat-k, which asks: if you run the same task k times, does the agent succeed on *all* of them? What you see is that even strong models with a decent pass^1 drop off quite sharply as k grows. That gap tells you something important: the model has the capability, but it doesn't have the reliability. And for deployment, reliability is often what matters.

More broadly, I think evaluation should start from the question: what does the real-world utility function look like? Different applications have very different shapes. In creative work or research exploration, the upside of one great output dominates, so you want to measure the best case. In high-stakes, repetitive, user-facing workflows, the downside dominates, so you want to measure the worst case, or consistency across many trials. Some settings are in between, where a human reviews the output and an error is cheap to catch, so moderate reliability is fine.

There's also the question of *what kind* of failure it is. Failing by saying "I'm not sure, let me transfer you to a human" is very different from confidently doing the wrong thing, like issuing a refund that violates policy. A good evaluation should distinguish those, because in practice the cost of the second is much higher.

So my view is that we need to move from asking "how smart is this model?" to asking "how much value does this agent create in a specific environment, with specific users and rules?" That means benchmarks that include realistic interaction, with simulated users who are ambiguous or change their minds, domain policies the agent must follow, and metrics that reflect the actual cost structure of mistakes. If our evaluations don't reflect that, we'll keep making progress on numbers that don't translate into products people trust.

r001.rationale: The response says pass@k asks whether the agent succeeds at least once and says this suits coding competitions.

r002.rationale: It says customer-service users need the agent to succeed every time, matching an all-K-attempts objective.

r003.rationale: It links the long-standing default pass@k metric to coding competitions and contrasts that benchmark-like framing with practical applications where reliability matters.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest starting point is that most of our benchmarks today measure something closer to "can the agent do this at all" rather than "can I actually trust this agent to do this." And those are very different questions once you leave the research setting.

If you look at how we usually report results, it's pass at one, or sometimes pass at k, averaged over a bunch of tasks. That tells you about capability. But a real application has a very specific reliability requirement baked into it. If I'm using an agent to draft a reply to an email, and it's wrong one time out of ten, that's fine, I'll just fix it. If I'm using an agent to execute a transaction or modify a production database, one in ten is completely unacceptable. You'd want something like one in ten thousand. The same model, the same average score, can be deployable in one case and useless in the other.

So one thing I've been pushing for is that we should look at the opposite of pass at k, which is something like pass to the k, meaning the probability that the agent succeeds on all k attempts, or consistently across k trials of the same task. That's a much better proxy for reliability. And what's interesting is that when you measure it this way, a lot of the progress we see in headline numbers kind of evaporates. Models that look close on pass at one can be very far apart on pass to the eight or pass to the sixteen, because consistency is a different property from peak capability.

The second piece is that the evaluation itself should be shaped by the application. In Tau-bench, for example, we deliberately built in a simulated user and a set of domain policies, because in customer service the hard part isn't solving the problem, it's solving it while following the rules and dealing with an ambiguous human. Those constraints are the reliability requirement. An agent that's clever but occasionally violates a refund policy is worse in practice than one that's slightly less capable but never does. So the benchmark has to encode what "failure" actually means in that domain, not just whether the final answer is correct.

And then third, I think we need to be more honest about the cost of errors being asymmetric. Most benchmarks treat every task the same, every failure the same. In reality some failures are recoverable and some are catastrophic. Evaluation that reflects practical requirements should at least distinguish between "didn't finish the task" and "did something it shouldn't have done." Those should probably be separate axes.

The broader point is that I think the field has been a bit too capability-obsessed. For a long time that was the right focus, because the agents couldn't do much. But now that they can do a lot, the bottleneck for actually getting value out of them is reliability, and our evaluation hasn't caught up. If I were designing a benchmark today, I'd care less about whether the model can occasionally do something impressive and much more about the variance, the worst case, and whether it stays within the constraints of the environment. That's what determines whether anyone will actually deploy it.

r001.rationale: It discusses pass-at-k generally as a capability measure, but does not identify that objective as appropriate for coding tasks.

r002.rationale: It recommends pass-to-k as a general measure of consistency and discusses customer-service constraints, but does not connect success on every attempt specifically to customer-service agents.

r003.rationale: It says current benchmarks emphasize whether an agent can do a task over whether it can be trusted in real applications, and describes the field as capability-obsessed, linking that emphasis to the lack of practical reliability evaluation.

astra-6.text:
I think we should start from the application and ask: what does a failure actually cost? If an agent recommends a restaurant, an occasional bad suggestion may be acceptable. If it performs a financial transaction, the reliability requirement is much higher. A single average success rate doesn’t capture that difference.

We also need to distinguish between producing something a person will review and taking an action directly. An agent might be useful at a relatively low success rate if people can quickly check its work. But if it operates autonomously over many steps, even a small failure probability at each step can become a serious problem.

So evaluation should measure more than whether the task was completed. Did the agent make an irreversible mistake? Did it recognize uncertainty and ask for help? Could it recover when something went wrong? And how much human supervision did it require?

Ultimately, the question is whether the agent is reliable enough for a particular role under particular constraints. Different applications should have different thresholds, and our evaluations should make those differences explicit.

r001.rationale: It discusses reliability for practical roles but does not identify success on at least one of K attempts as an evaluation objective for coding tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not identify success on every one of K attempts as an evaluation objective for customer-service agents.

r003.rationale: It recommends application-specific evaluation but does not attribute current evaluations’ limited emphasis on robustness to their focus on benchmark tasks over practical applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start with the application, because reliability means different things in different settings. If an agent recommends a restaurant, an occasional mistake may be acceptable. If it handles a financial transaction, the tolerance for mistakes is much lower, and some actions should require human confirmation.

So a single average success rate is not enough. We need to ask: What kinds of failures happen? How costly are they? Can the agent recognize uncertainty, ask for help, and recover? Two agents might both succeed 90 percent of the time, but one fails harmlessly while the other makes irreversible mistakes. Those are very different systems in practice.

We should also evaluate the whole workflow, including the human involvement and the time and cost needed to reach a reliable result. The goal is to understand which tasks we can actually delegate, under what conditions, and with what level of supervision.
